messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: hierarchical model with binary outcome
parts:
Dear List,

I am working on a hierarchical model of child mortality (0/1).  Observations (N = 408,706) are nested within mothers (n = 141,999), cities (n = 3,806), districts (n = 443), and states (n = 26).  The outcome is quite unequal, with about 91.4% 0s and 8.6% 1s.

I would love any feedback on how tractable working with data of this size is in Stan.  Right now, I am trying a simple intercept only model, which I tried parameterizing two different ways.

To Stan's credit, both seem to be running.  The time it takes for a single iteration is a bit too long though --- a few minutes for 1 iteration.  Even if the effective sample size was exactly the number of iterations, it would take a couple days to get to 1,000, even in this simple model.  Suggestions would be welcome, it also may just be unrealistic to run multiple levels with this much data quickly.

Cheers,

Josh (code below):


First a simple way, about how I would think about the model/equations:

# simple way
data {
  int<lower=0> n4;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> N;


  int<lower=1, upper=n4> ID4[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n3> ID3[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n2> ID2[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n1> ID1[N];


  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_1;
  real<lower=0> sigma_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_3;
  real<lower=0> sigma_4;


  vector[n4] int_4;
  vector[n3] int_3;
  vector[n2] int_2;
  vector[n1] int_1;
  real intercept;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] p;


  for (i in 1:N) {
    p[i] <- inv_logit(intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]]);
  }
}
model {
  sigma_4 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_3 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0, 2);


  int_4 ~ normal(0, sigma_4);
  int_3 ~ normal(0, sigma_3);
  int_2 ~ normal(0, sigma_2);
  int_1 ~ normal(0, sigma_1);
  intercept ~ normal(0, 3);


  y ~ bernoulli(p);
}


And here trying to reparameterize to scale and shift the parameters so the priors come from N(0, 1).

# Shift and Scale Approach
data {

  int<lower=0> n4;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> N;


  int<lower=1, upper=n4> ID4[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n3> ID3[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n2> ID2[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n1> ID1[N];


  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_1;
  real<lower=0> sigma_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_3;
  real<lower=0> sigma_4;


  vector[n4] int_4raw;
  vector[n3] int_3raw;
  vector[n2] int_2raw;
  vector[n1] int_1raw;
  real intercept;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] p;
  vector[n4] int_4;
  vector[n3] int_3;
  vector[n2] int_2;
  vector[n1] int_1;


  int_4 <- sigma_4 * int_4raw;
  int_3 <- sigma_3 * int_3raw;
  int_2 <- sigma_2 * int_2raw;
  int_1 <- sigma_1 * int_1raw;


  for (i in 1:N) {
    p[i] <- intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]];
  }
}
model {
  sigma_4 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_3 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0, 2);


  int_4raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_3raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_2raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_1raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  intercept ~ normal(0, 3);


  y ~ bernoulli_logit(p);
}

My first question would be: Do you include compilation in your running time? 

Some of my model can easily take up to >20 minutes to compile and run for a few iterations (25-50 samples). However, once the model is compiled the numbers of iterations by hours is much more reasonable. A model with a few thousands iteration is bound to take some time to compile... 

Chris
----------------------

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical model with binary outcome
parts:
I'd recommend removing the transformed parameter block, and replacing
the sampling statement in the model block with:
for (i in 1:N)

p[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]]);

Using vector arguments doesn't speed up bernoulli(_logit) as there are
no shared parameters.

Your model's only identified through priors, which can cause
substantial computational slowdown if the priors aren't particularly
tight. It's OK to center them all around zero and push the means into
the shared intercept.

If you've fit the data using some other GLM software, you might want
to see what the values are for coefficients to make sure the prior for
the intercept is reasonable.

Even if this doesn't give you a big speedup, you may not need 1000 iterations.
You only need to run until your MCMC std error is below where you want it.
And you can run in parallel if you have enough memory, though you have a very
large number of parameters (150K just for the mothers!), which could be prohibitive.

Run time will be much slower during warmup, then go faster per iteration
after that. You might also not need much warmup for this model, but I'm
guessing the mother parameters are going to be relatively hard to identify
given the low counts per mother.

And if worse comes to worst, 1000 minutes is still less than 24 hours :-)

- Bob

And here trying to reparameterize to scale and shift the parameters so the priors come from N(0, 1).

# Shift and Scale Approach
data {

  int<lower=0> n4;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> N;


  int<lower=1, upper=n4> ID4[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n3> ID3[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n2> ID2[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=n1> ID1[N];


  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_1;
  real<lower=0> sigma_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_3;
  real<lower=0> sigma_4;


  vector[n4] int_4raw;
  vector[n3] int_3raw;
  vector[n2] int_2raw;
  vector[n1] int_1raw;
  real intercept;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] p;
  vector[n4] int_4;
  vector[n3] int_3;
  vector[n2] int_2;
  vector[n1] int_1;


  int_4 <- sigma_4 * int_4raw;
  int_3 <- sigma_3 * int_3raw;
  int_2 <- sigma_2 * int_2raw;
  int_1 <- sigma_1 * int_1raw;


  for (i in 1:N) {
    p[i] <- intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]];
  }
}
model {
  sigma_4 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_3 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0, 2);


  int_4raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_3raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_2raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  int_1raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  intercept ~ normal(0, 3);


  y ~ bernoulli_logit(p);
}

parts:
Compile time only depends on the size of the model specification,
and the complexity of operations involved (inverse wishart is more
compile intense than addition), but does not depend on the size of
the data.

Reading data into the model will depend on the size of the data, but
that's only done once.

In addition, the 9% vs. 91% balance isn't enough to worry about. Should
be no problem for logistic regression.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical model with binary outcome
parts:
Thanks!  These are very helpful suggestions, and good to know about bernoulli(_logit) and vectorization.

I have run this model in MCMCglmm in R before, so have some other numbers for reference.

I am trying these suggestions out and will post back how it goes.

Thanks! :)
On Thu, Aug 14, 2014 at 10:53 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

I'd recommend removing the transformed parameter block, and replacing
the sampling statement in the model block with:

  for (i in 1:N)
    p[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]]);

Using vector arguments doesn't speed up bernoulli(_logit) as there are
no shared parameters.

Your model's only identified through priors, which can cause
substantial computational slowdown if the priors aren't particularly
tight.  It's OK to center them all around zero and push the means into
the shared intercept.

If you've fit the data using some other GLM software, you might want
to see what the values are for coefficients to make sure the prior for
the intercept is reasonable.

Even if this doesn't give you a big speedup, you may not need 1000 iterations.
You only need to run until your MCMC std error is below where you want it.
And you can run in parallel if you have enough memory, though you have a very
large number of parameters (150K just for the mothers!), which could be prohibitive.

Run time will be much slower during warmup, then go faster per iteration
after that.  You might also not need much warmup for this model, but I'm
guessing the mother parameters are going to be relatively hard to identify
given the low counts per mother.

And if worse comes to worst, 1000 minutes is still less than 24 hours :-)

- Bob

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: hierarchical model with binary outcome
parts:
Hi Joshua,

From your code, I understand (and correct me if I'm wrong) that you are not using individual level predictors, right? If you are sticking to this intercept-only model, you could crank down significantly on computation by collapsing you data from (0/1) bernoulli responses to (k/N_kids) binomial responses, where N_kids is the number of children a mother had, and k is the number of kids that died. Then just model the binomial likelihood instead of the bernoulli:

for (i in 1:N_mothers)
    k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N_kids[i], intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]]);

If on average mothers in your data have 2 kids, this means that you can compress your data (and number of likelihood evaluations) by a factor two. If at some point, you want to add individual-level predictors and these predictors are categorical (e.g. gender), you might to still apply aggregation, but now at the level of kid-gender | mother. Of course, if the number of kids per mother is low, this won't really have a significant impact.

Good luck,

Luc

parts:
The binomial should be quite a bit faster --- it saves doing multiple
additions and inverse-logit calculations, which is where the
time's going to be spent in this model. It does add some multiplications,
though. So it'll be interesting to me to see what the difference is if
the average N_kids is 2.

- Bob
